newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Maskhadov on course for Chechen poll victory. [CORRECTED 10:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Maskhadov on course for Chechen poll victory. [CORRECTED 10:40 GMT]

text.p: Aslan Maskhadov, who forced Russian troops out of Chechnya with a combination of guerrilla warfare and shrewd diplomacy, appeared headed on Tuesday for a clear victory in presidential elections.
At Maskhadov's headquarters in the Chechen capital, Grozny, guerrillas in camouflage uniform with rifles slung over their shoulders hugged each other as women laughed and celebrated.

"Preliminary figures allow us to say that Aslan Maskhadov has become president of Chechnya," said Maskhadov's closest aide and spokesman Mayerbek Vachagayev as he raised a clenched fist in the air in a victory gesture following Monday's poll.

The claim, if confirmed by official results, might offer some comfort in Moscow after a disastrous military campaign, although he has vowed to confront the Kremlin over the delicate issue of the mainly Moslem region's sovereignty.

As the man who inflicted humiliating defeats on the Russian army he is surely no friend of the Kremlin. But among 13 candidates in Monday's poll, the quietly spoken former Soviet army colonel is the man Russian leaders have learned to deal with at the negotiating table.

Vachagayev said early results showed Maskhadov had captured about 58 percent, against 30 percent for chief rival Shamil Basayev. If no candidate wins 50 percent in the first round, a second ballot will be held between the two top candidates.

Maskhadov negotiated a peace deal with Moscow last year, providing for complete withdrawal of Russian troops after a two-year war that resulted in tens of thousands of dead and widespread destruction in Chechnya.
About a kilometre (mile) away from Maskhadov's headquarters, near the Minutka traffic roundabout that was long a focus of fighting, the mood in rival Shamil Basayev's camp was sombre.
A Basayev victory would be a further bitter blow for the Kremlin which sees him without reservation as a terrorist.

Basayev (corrects from Shamiyev) led a raid on the south Russian town of Budennovsk in 1995, taking some 1,000 hostages. About 100 people died in the action, which revived a flagging guerrilla campaign.

All leading candidates say they would press quickly for sovereignty, despite a provision in the peace deal deferring the issue for five years. Maskhadov demands "war reparations" to rebuild an economy based on the oil industry.

A Russian Deputy Foreign Minister, underlining Kremlin sensitivity on the sovereignty issue, said at the weekend that Moscow was ready to break off relations with any country that moved to grant Chechnya diplomatic recognition.
Another leading Maskhadov rival, Movladi Udugov, virtually acknowledged defeat.

"It's time to finish with the dividing up of power and get down to work," he said, in a clear indication he would be willing to co-operate with Maskhadov to prevent any future internal conflict. Maskhadov seemed to be sure of victory.

The present acting President Zemlikhan Yandarbiyev said he would not work with Maskhadov. "There is no precedent in history for an outgoing president to work with the new one," he told the Moscow radio station Ekho Moskvy.
Electoral Commission Chairman Mumadi Saydaiyev told Russian Television Maskhadov had more than 60 percent by early morning. A preliminary result may be available towards evening, he said.
In Moscow, President Boris Yeltsin, recovering from pneumonia, called a meeting of his top-level Consultative Council to discuss the results of the poll on Tuesday.
Outside observers have said they were impressed by the smoothness of the voting and an absence of major violations.
There were no reports of violence in a land awash with arms.

Yeltsin admits sending troops to crush the Chechen rebels in 1994 ranks as one of the biggest mistakes of his presidency. It could yet be one that haunts him well into a second term already overshadowed by illness.
Chechens in their devastated capital Grozny voiced mixed emotions about the prospect of Maskhadov as their leader.
"I think that today Maskhadov is the best man to stabilise the situation in Chechnya," said one young voter.
"Now they (Russia) will have to recognise us, we're people too, like Portugal, Holland, we're not monkeys," said another. "With Maskhadov as president everything will be OK."
But another armed man sporting the black beard of a Moslem guerrilla, feared Maskhadov would be "too soft" on Moscow.
"He may be a soldier, but he's weak," he said. "The people who voted for Maskhadov are opposed to independence."
Maskhadov's task will be far from simple.
Chechnya has won de facto independence with the withdrawal of Russian troops. But with its back to the towering Caucasus mountains, it is hemmed in by Russian territory and is all but bankrupt.
